Series lineage Semiconductor Foundry Technologies x Intelligent Nanomanufacturing - Flagship 23 Publication Abstract This monograph examines whether microrobotic sampling and semiconductor biochips can increase useful spatial and temporal diagnostic information without changing the sampled state or concealing failure inside an end-to-end model. It follows every specimen from agent identity, position, time, force, and volume through recovery, transport, adsorption, carryover, preprocessing, chip lot, surface chemistry, raw transduction, calibration, multimodal fusion, uncertainty, and independent reference adjudication. The central falsifiable proposition is that joint calibration of sampling and analysis should improve information under the same specimen, time, disturbance, instrument, and operator budget as fixed microfluidic sampling, expert manual sampling, and validated laboratory methods. If an apparent gain comes from more sampling, hidden exclusions, shared preprocessing, matrix bias, carryover, noncommutable standards, or threshold tuning, the broader diagnostic claim is rejected or narrowed. Scientific Position and Hard Boundary Research-platform performance, analytical validity, diagnostic accuracy, clinical utility, and medical decision authority are separate claim levels. A precise trajectory does not prove sample integrity. A sensitive chip does not prove diagnostic accuracy. Agreement between correlated modalities does not prove independent confirmation. No chapter authorizes autonomous medical decisions, treatment, or human deployment. Candidate Research Expression Dinfo = information over location, time, and analyte x sample-chain validity - carryover - matrix bias - decision risk • Sample identity, position, time, and volume remain traceable at every stage. • Recovery and mass balance include dead volume, adsorption, residuals, dilution, and storage loss. • Semiconductor readout is qualified with blanks, standards, internal references, raw signals, and full wafer or lot denominators. • Multimodal gain is conditional on information already supplied by other modalities and preprocessing. • Safety, broken identity, missing reference evidence, uncontrolled contamination, and unsupported medical claims are hard vetoes. Five Layer Research Architecture 01 Analyte Sample Chain and Decision Boundary Define analyte, intended use, identity, location, time, preprocessing, reference method, repeat rules, and downstream decision limits. 02 Microrobotic Volume Position and Disturbance Calibrate sampling envelope, coordinate uncertainty, recovered volume, wall interaction, local depletion, actuation, and safe recovery. 03 Semiconductor Preprocessing and Multimodal Readout Bind the sample to chip lot, surface chemistry, calibration ancestor, raw readout, and modality-specific uncertainty. 04 Contamination Interference and Unknown Challenges Inject swaps, carryover, matrix effects, cross-reactivity, reagent drift, unknown interferents, and reference disagreement. 05 Blind Reference Adjudication and Successor Transfer Require locked thresholds, independent methods, full denominators, cross-site reconstruction, and deliberate retirement of unsupported claims. Minimum Verifiable Prototype A microfluidic challenge platform hides analyte gradients and interferents across known but masked locations. Microrobotic, fixed, and expert manual sampling are compared under matched specimen, time, disturbance, calibration, and operator budgets. Every sample is bound to a coordinate and custody record, analyzed on a CMOS biochip, and adjudicated by an independent laboratory method. Sequential high-to-blank challenges, matrix substitutions, sample swaps, unknown interferents, chip-lot drift, and forced abstention test the entire chain. Research Contributions • Replaces isolated chip accuracy with chain-complete diagnostic information. • Connects microrobotic sampling physics, mass balance, surface chemistry, semiconductor transduction, matrix effects, calibration, and diagnostic study design. • Maps thirty distinct derivations to chapter, experiment, and Research Gate corridors. • Provides eighty-two chapters with five research pages per chapter. • Turns two hundred Research Gates into detailed future-study cards with evidence, stop conditions, and Microrobotic Diagnostic Chain Passports. • Preserves fixed sampling, manual sampling, single-modality assays, and centralized laboratories as legitimate winners. • Makes repeat, reference-wins, and abstain valid outcomes. • Separates analytical performance, diagnostic accuracy, clinical utility, and medical decision authority. What the Book Does Not Claim The monograph does not report a completed clinical diagnostic trial, autonomous medical system, or newly established disease test. Synthetic and organ-on-chip matrices have limited external validity. Independent reference methods can also be uncertain. Rare preanalytical failures may remain unobserved. Human diagnostic use requires separate ethics, regulation, quality systems, privacy, cybersecurity, prospective validation, and clinical governance. Series lineage Semiconductor Foundry Technologies x Intelligent Nanomanufacturing - Flagship 20 Publication Abstract This monograph asks whether an autonomous foundry laboratory can do more than optimize an existing recipe. It develops a research architecture in which the system must register competing process mechanisms, identify what its sensors can and cannot distinguish, choose experiments for model discrimination, preserve negative evidence, and issue counterfactual predictions that survive a new tool or fab. Yield improvement, simulation fit, and automation speed are treated as useful engineering outcomes but not as proof of a new mechanism. The central falsifiable proposition is that active experiments chosen to separate rival predictions should reduce the set of observationally equivalent mechanisms and improve preregistered counterfactual forecasts under the same sample, metrology, time, energy, and safety budget as expert DOE and strong safe Bayesian optimization. If the experiment cannot distinguish the models, if failures are selectively forgotten, if the acquisition function exploits a biased proxy, or if cross-tool predictions fail, the scientific claim is narrowed, split, or stopped. Scientific Position and Hard Boundary The work begins with bounded thin-film, deposition, etch, interface, and defect-mechanism challenges in simulation, digital-physical twins, test vehicles, and low-risk equipment states. Autonomous execution is permitted only through typed process intent, equipment capability contracts, explicit authorization, independent metrology, abort logic, and recoverable physical states. No information-gain score may override safety, material irreversibility, chain of custody, environmental obligations, worker protection, or equipment interlocks. Candidate Research Expression Dsci = Delta H of competing models + counterfactual information - sample cost - unsafe risk - hype penalty • Delta H measures reduction in uncertainty over the preregistered mechanism set. • Counterfactual information rewards predictions about interventions or new platforms that were not used for fitting. • Sample cost includes material, metrology, time, energy, and opportunity cost. • Unsafe risk is a hard feasibility concern, not a term that can be purchased by predicted knowledge. • The hype penalty prevents an engineering improvement from being narrated as a causal discovery. Five Layer Research Architecture 01 Competing Mechanism Contract Register rival mechanisms, observable signatures, claim levels, strong baselines, and hard boundaries. 02 Observability and Evidence Graph Map sensors, latent state, calibration ancestry, identifiability, and equivalent model sets. 03 Discriminating Active Experiment Choose controls, interventions, and fidelities for information under sample, energy, and risk budgets. 04 Refutation Memory and Safe Execution Compile typed experiments, preserve failures, detect misspecification, abort safely, and record why models were rejected. 05 Independent Transfer and Successor Choice Demand cross-tool counterfactual predictions, third-party replay, and the right to split, downgrade, or retire a mechanism. Minimum Verifiable Prototype Two process mechanisms are constructed to explain the same historical thin-film or etch observations. Expert DOE, safe Bayesian optimization, and the autonomous discovery policy receive matched samples, metrology, wall time, energy, and safety envelopes. Before the hidden outcomes are revealed, each freezes its hypotheses, predicted signatures, next experiment, acquisition value, uncertainty, and stopping rule. The decisive test is whether independent terminal metrology and a new intervention eliminate or sharply narrow one mechanism, not whether the system merely finds a better recipe. Research Contributions • Separates optimization, prediction, mechanism discrimination, causal support, and cross-platform scientific claims. • Connects observability, identifiability, Fisher information, Bayesian experimental design, causal intervention, and model criticism. • Treats negative results, failed experiments, calibration ancestry, manual corrections, and eliminated models as first-class scientific records. • Maps thirty distinct derivations to chapter, experiment, and Research Gate corridors. • Provides eighty-two chapters with five research pages per chapter: boundary, identifiability, minimum test, adversarial refutation, and successor route. • Turns two hundred Research Gates into detailed future-study cards with a strong baseline, evidence packet, stop condition, and reconstruction invitation. • Allows expert DOE or a simpler Bayesian optimizer to remain the stronger answer. • Defines success as transferable, refutable knowledge rather than publication volume or autonomous activity. What the Book Does Not Claim The monograph does not report a completed autonomous fab deployment and does not imply that every process has a uniquely identifiable mechanism. Digital twins can omit decisive state, active learning can exploit a wrong model class, and cross-tool failure may reveal a hidden context variable. Physical deployment requires site-specific engineering validation, material and equipment safety review, worker consultation, cybersecurity, quality-system approval, complete negative-result custody, and accountable human authority.
